sets.title: Birthday boat trip
sets.passage:
Hi Lissa,

My birthday is on Sunday, and this year I don't want a party at home. Instead, my uncle has offered to take four of us across Lake Urren in his little motorboat. We will stop at the small island in the middle, have a picnic lunch there and swim if the water is warm enough. We leave from the boat club at ten and come back by four. Can you come? Please bring a towel and a warm jacket, because it gets windy on the water.

Kasper

sets.title: Coach on a different road
sets.passage:
Hi Luka,

Just a quick update from the school trip. Our coach was supposed to reach the mountain hostel by lunchtime, but the main road was closed after a rockfall last night. The police diverted all the traffic onto a narrow road through the village of Lakeby, so we are moving much more slowly. The teachers think we will arrive around five instead of one. Everyone is fine, and the views are amazing. I will send you some photos tonight!

Kiri

sets.title: How train wheels take a bend
sets.passage:
When a car turns a corner, its outside wheels must travel farther than its inside wheels. A car solves this with a set of gears that lets each wheel turn at its own speed. The wheels of a train cannot do this. Each pair is fixed to one solid steel bar called an axle, so both wheels always turn together.

So how does a train get around a bend? The answer is in the shape of its wheels. The part of a train wheel that touches the rail is not flat. It is shaped like a slice of a cone, slightly wider near the inside of the wheel and narrower toward the outside.

On a curve, the train drifts a little toward the outside of the bend. This makes the outer wheel roll on its wider part and the inner wheel roll on its narrower part. In one full turn, a wide circle covers more ground than a narrow one, so the outer wheel travels farther even though both wheels turn at the same rate.

The same shape also keeps a train centred on straight track. If the train slips to one side, the wheels on that side roll on their wider part and steer it back toward the middle. Each wheel also has a raised rim on its inner edge, but this is mainly a safety feature for sharp curves. On most track, the cone shape does the steering.

sets.title: A map for newcomers
sets.passage:
Our school has three buildings joined by long corridors, and every September the new students get lost. Last year I was one of them. On my first day I walked into a music lesson instead of maths and sat through twenty minutes of singing before I found the courage to leave.

This year our teacher, Ms. Kellaway, asked our class to make a better map for the newcomers. The old one was a plan an architect had drawn, full of tiny room numbers. We decided to walk the buildings ourselves and draw what a lost student would actually see: the blue doors near the library, the noisy drinks machine, the stairs covered in old team photos.

We tested our first version on a group of younger students. We gave each of them the map and three rooms to find, and we followed them without speaking. Most of them went the wrong way at the same corner, because we had drawn the art room on the wrong side. After we fixed that, every student in our second test found all three rooms in under ten minutes.

Copies of our map now hang by every main entrance. A boy called Uskar, who joined in October, told me he had used it every day for a week. I never told him about my music lesson.

sets.title: The green posts of Lunford
sets.passage:
In the 1830s the town of Lunford, a busy river port of about twelve thousand people, had grown too long for comfortable walking. Its docks lay at the southern end, its market and offices at the northern end, and the workers who lived near one often had to reach the other. A private carriage was far beyond the means of a dock labourer or a shop assistant, so most people simply walked, sometimes for an hour in each direction.

In 1834 a carpenter named Kester Larkham built a long wooden carriage with benches along both sides, hitched it to two horses, and began driving it up and down Kemble Street, the road that joined the two ends of town. Anyone could ride for a penny. Within a month his vehicle was carrying several hundred passengers a day, and Larkham had ordered a second one.

Success quickly created a problem. Larkham's drivers stopped wherever someone raised a hand, so a journey that should have taken twenty minutes could stretch to fifty. Regular riders complained that they could never predict when they would arrive at work, and some went back to walking. Larkham's answer was to paint a dozen wooden posts bright green and set them along Kemble Street at roughly equal distances. From then on, the carriages would halt only at a post, and a printed card in every carriage listed the times at which each post would be reached.

Not everyone welcomed the posts. Several shopkeepers on Kemble Street had enjoyed having customers step down directly outside their doors, and they argued that a stop in front of a rival's window would ruin them. Lisbet Umber, who sold hats near the middle of the street, collected the names of forty traders on a letter asking the town council to remove the posts. The council, which had little power over a private business, declined to act, but it suggested that Larkham meet the traders himself.

The meeting produced a compromise that pleased few people at first. Larkham kept his posts but agreed to move three of them so that each stood between two shops rather than in front of one. Within a year, however, the traders had changed their minds. Passengers waiting at a post had several minutes to fill, and they spent them looking into the nearest windows. The shops closest to the green posts did noticeably better than before, and by 1840 Umber herself was paying Larkham a small fee each year to have a post placed outside her door.

Larkham's green posts are often described as the first fixed stops in the region. Whether or not that is true, they show how quickly a convenience can become part of daily life: within a generation, the people of Lunford gave directions by them, telling visitors to walk two posts north of the bridge or to wait at the fifth post.

sets.title: The number 12
sets.passage:
Una had planned the trip for a week. Her grandfather Konrad wanted to see the new exhibition of old city photographs at the museum on Kipp Street, and her mother had asked Una to take him, since his eyes were now too weak for him to read the small print on timetables. Una had downloaded a travel app, saved the route and checked it twice: tram 4 from the stop outside his flat, a change at Lindgate Square, then tram 9 to the museum door. Thirty-five minutes in all. It was the first time she had been in charge of a whole trip.

At Lindgate Square the screen above the platform flashed a message in red: tram 9 was suspended because of repairs on the line. Other passengers were already walking away. Una stared at her phone. The app still showed tram 9 running every ten minutes, as if nothing had happened. She refreshed it four times. Her grandfather, meanwhile, had sat down on a bench and was surveying the square with an expression she could only describe as amused.

"Repairs on the Keeling Bridge, probably," he said. "They always do that bridge in October." He stood up and pointed across the square. "Take the 12 to the old fish market. From there it is a five-minute walk along the river, and the museum is on the corner. I drove the 12 for nineteen years, long before you were born."

Una had known, in a general way, that her grandfather had once worked on the trams. It was one of those family facts that are mentioned at birthdays and then forgotten. She had never imagined that the city's lines might still be stored in his head, stop by stop, like a song he had learned as a child.

They took the 12. Her grandfather named each stop a second before the recorded voice did, and twice he told her about buildings that were no longer there: a cinema where a supermarket now stood, and a bakery that had sold bread shaped like horseshoes. At the fish market he set off along the river so quickly that she had to hurry to keep up.

The exhibition filled two rooms. Near the end of the second, Konrad stopped in front of a large black-and-white photograph of a tram crossing a bridge in heavy snow. He leaned so close that his nose almost touched the glass, and then he asked Una to read him the small card beside it. She read it aloud: tram 12 on the Keeling Bridge during a snowstorm many winters ago, photographer unknown.

"Number thirty-one," he said quietly. "I was driving it."

On the way home, Una kept her phone in her pocket and let him choose the route.

He had read about the bridge repairs in the newspaper.
He wanted to go home as soon as he heard about tram 9.
He felt no surprise at the red message on the screen.
items.correct_answer: He felt no surprise at the red message on the screen.
items.why: They always do that bridge in October
items.why2: was surveying the square with an expression she could only describe as amused
items.explanation: "He felt no surprise at the red message on the screen." is correct: he looked "amused" while Una was worried, and he explained that "They always do that bridge in October", so the closure was something he expected.

distractor_rationales.choice: He wanted to go home as soon as he heard about tram 9.
distractor_rationales.reason: "He wanted to go home as soon as he heard about tram 9." is contradicted: "He stood up and pointed across the square" and gave a new route to the museum.

distractor_rationales.choice: He needed Una's phone to work out another way there.
distractor_rationales.reason: "He needed Una's phone to work out another way there." is contradicted: he gave the route from memory, "I drove the 12 for nineteen years".

distractor_rationales.choice: He had read about the bridge repairs in the newspaper.
distractor_rationales.reason: "He had read about the bridge repairs in the newspaper." is contradicted: he only guesses, "Repairs on the Keeling Bridge, probably," and "his eyes were now too weak for him to read the small print".

items.prompt: In the museum, what did Konrad ask Una to do?
choices: take a picture of the photograph for him
describe the tram in the picture to him
find out who had taken the photograph
read the words on the small card to him
items.correct_answer: read the words on the small card to him
items.why: he asked Una to read him the small card beside it
items.explanation: "read the words on the small card to him" is correct: the story says "he asked Una to read him the small card beside it", and "She read it aloud".

distractor_rationales.choice: take a picture of the photograph for him
distractor_rationales.reason: "take a picture of the photograph for him" is never asked; the story says "he asked Una to read him the small card beside it".

distractor_rationales.choice: find out who had taken the photograph
distractor_rationales.reason: "find out who had taken the photograph" reuses the card's words; the card itself says "photographer unknown", and what he asked was for Una "to read him the small card beside it".

distractor_rationales.choice: describe the tram in the picture to him
distractor_rationales.reason: "describe the tram in the picture to him" is not what he asked; he looked himself, "He leaned so close that his nose almost touched the glass", and then asked her "to read him the small card".

items.prompt: Why does the writer mention the cinema and the bakery in paragraph 5?
choices: to give an example of how the trams themselves have changed
to suggest that Konrad was confused about where they were
to show that Una had seen these places on her app
to show how much of the old city Konrad recalls
items.correct_answer: to show how much of the old city Konrad recalls
items.why: twice he told her about buildings that were no longer there
items.explanation: "to show how much of the old city Konrad recalls" is correct: Konrad "told her about buildings that were no longer there", which shows his memory of the city, like the lines "stored in his head, stop by stop".

distractor_rationales.choice: to show that Una had seen these places on her app
distractor_rationales.reason: "to show that Una had seen these places on her app" is wrong: these were "buildings that were no longer there", and it was Konrad who "told her about" them.

distractor_rationales.choice: to give an example of how the trams themselves have changed
distractor_rationales.reason: "to give an example of how the trams themselves have changed" confuses buildings with trams: "a cinema where a supermarket now stood, and a bakery".

distractor_rationales.choice: to suggest that Konrad was confused about where they were
distractor_rationales.reason: "to suggest that Konrad was confused about where they were" is contradicted in the same paragraph: he "named each stop a second before the recorded voice did".

items.prompt: In paragraph 2, the word "surveying" is closest in meaning to
choices: measuring the land
valuing a building
polling the public
looking over carefully
items.correct_answer: looking over carefully
items.why: was surveying the square with an expression she could only describe as amused
items.explanation: "looking over carefully" is correct: he sat on a bench "surveying the square", watching it, and then "pointed across the square" to the right tram.

distractor_rationales.choice: measuring the land
distractor_rationales.reason: "measuring the land" is a meaning for map-makers; he is sitting "on a bench" and simply looking at "the square" before he "pointed across the square".

distractor_rationales.choice: polling the public
distractor_rationales.reason: "polling the public" is a meaning for opinion research; he asks nobody anything, and he looks at the square "with an expression she could only describe as amused".

distractor_rationales.choice: valuing a building
distractor_rationales.reason: "valuing a building" is a meaning for house sales; the thing he looks at is "the square", not a building, and he is sitting "on a bench".

items.prompt: Why does the story end with Una keeping her phone in her pocket?
choices: to suggest that Konrad told her to stop checking the app
to show that Konrad can now read timetables for himself
to show that Una wants to take the same trams home again
to show that Una is now happy to let her grandfather guide them both
items.correct_answer: to show that Una is now happy to let her grandfather guide them both
items.why: let him choose the route
items.explanation: "to show that Una is now happy to let her grandfather guide them both" is correct: after he found a new route and recognised his own tram ("I was driving it"), Una "kept her phone in her pocket and let him choose the route".

distractor_rationales.choice: to show that Una wants to take the same trams home again
distractor_rationales.reason: "to show that Una wants to take the same trams home again" is wrong: she does not choose the route; she "let him choose the route".

distractor_rationales.choice: to suggest that Konrad told her to stop checking the app
distractor_rationales.reason: "to suggest that Konrad told her to stop checking the app" is wrong: the story gives no such order; Una herself "kept her phone in her pocket and let him choose the route".

distractor_rationales.choice: to show that Konrad can now read timetables for himself
distractor_rationales.reason: "to show that Konrad can now read timetables for himself" is contradicted: "his eyes were now too weak for him to read the small print on timetables", and in the museum he still "asked Una to read him the small card".
